sitemap.lede: Every section of this site on one page. The machine-readable version lives at sitemap.xml; this is the human one.

studyGuidesIndex.title: Study guides
studyGuidesIndex.lede: Two ways to study here, and they answer different questions. Curated reading paths follow a technology rather than an exam: read the Learn library in teaching order, with the tools to practise on as you go. Certification study guides live on their own page and do the opposite - they start from a vendor's published exam blueprint and map it objective by objective.
studyGuidesIndex.pathsLede: A path is a syllabus with no exam behind it. Nothing here is organised around a certification blueprint or scored against one: the order is the order the subject makes sense in, chosen so each article earns the next. Read straight through, or stop when you have what you came for. Everything computes locally and nothing is paywalled.
studyGuidesIndex.certLede: These are the exam-shaped ones, and they live on the certifications page. Each follows a vendor's own published blueprint objective by objective, tying every objective to the articles that teach it, the tools that exercise it, and the manual pages that remain the source of truth.

bigip-fundamentals.title: F5 BIG-IP end to end
bigip-fundamentals.lede: Everything the retired 101, 201, 301A, and 301B blueprints listed, as this site's articles in teaching order: the networking fundamentals the modern track assumes (OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) to VPN (virtual private network)), the full administration arc from interfaces to high availability to the support workflows the new exams dropped, and the LTM (Local Traffic Manager) specialist craft - iRules, analytics, captures, SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) - closing with the two articles that compare the retired blueprints against the current ones.

modern-identity.title: Modern identity, from the token up
modern-identity.lede: The open standards behind single sign-on, in dependency order: the JWT (JSON Web Token) itself, the signatures and JWKS (JSON Web Key Set) that make it verifiable, the OAuth 2.0 and PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) flows that mint it, OIDC (OpenID Connect) on top, and TOTP/HOTP (time-based and HMAC-based one-time passwords) as the second factor.

tls-from-zero.title: TLS from zero
tls-from-zero.lede: TLS (Transport Layer Security) from the cipher suite string upward: what each part of a suite name means, what TLS 1.3 removed and why, how hybrid post-quantum key exchange works, and how TLS 1.2, TLS 1.3, DTLS (Datagram TLS), and QUIC relate as one family.

http-evolution.title: HTTP, told forward
http-evolution.lede: HTTP (the Hypertext Transfer Protocol) across its five versions - from the one-line GET of 1991 to HTTP/3 on QUIC - then the operational layer: forward and reverse proxies, HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security), and curl beyond the browser.

regex-mastery.title: Regular expressions, properly
regex-mastery.lede: The craft skill under log analysis and every parser: quantifiers and classes, groups and backreferences, anchors and boundaries, flags and modes - ending on catastrophic backtracking, the failure mode every production regex must avoid.

pingfederate-administration.title: PingFederate administration, end to end
pingfederate-administration.lede: The blueprint's assumed fundamentals first - the directory model and the Kerberos ticket machinery - then the ten product articles in teaching order, SCIM beside the provisioning stop, and the SSO flows to close. The reading spine behind the PFP-001 certification guide.

zscaler-zero-trust.title: Zscaler Zero Trust Exchange
zscaler-zero-trust.lede: From tunnels and fundamentals to the full policy brain: forwarding, firewall order, TLS inspection, web and file controls, DLP, CASB, and ZPA's segments, policy, and posture — with the three native tools to practice on.

netskope-sase.title: Netskope SASE, End to End
netskope-sase.lede: The whole platform in reading order: architecture and NewEdge, every steering method, the client, TLS decryption, the two protection paths, CCI-driven policy, Private Access, Cloud Firewall, and the analytics layer - with the PAC and SAML tools to practice on. Built to walk the accreditation and certification domains from this site.

ping-identity-platform.title: The Ping Identity Platform
ping-identity-platform.lede: The whole Ping estate in reading order: the PingOne platform map and the ForgeRock lineage first, so every product name resolves; then PingAccess policy, the PingDirectory data platform, and DaVinci orchestration; closing with the PingFederate shelf - the self-managed federation core - in its established teaching order. The companion walk to the Certified Professional guides on the certifications hub.

checkpoint-security-administration.title: Check Point security administration
checkpoint-security-administration.lede: The platform in the order the CCSA teaches it: the three-tier split first, because nothing else makes sense until you know the management server and the gateway are different machines with different jobs, then the rule base, then the layer semantics that catch everyone.

nginx-from-config-to-cache.title: NGINX, from configuration to cache
nginx-from-config-to-cache.lede: In the order the confusions actually arrive: the configuration tree, then which location block wins, then what path the backend receives, then what gets cached and served to whom.

extreme-fabric-and-voss.title: Extreme fabric and the two operating systems
extreme-fabric-and-voss.lede: ExtremeXOS for the configuration model, then why VOSS feels so different (it came from another company entirely), then Fabric Connect built up from IS-IS through I-SIDs to the resilience features.

fortinet-fabric-and-operations.title: Fortinet beyond the single firewall
fortinet-fabric-and-operations.lede: What shows up once a FortiGate is not alone: inspection choices, the branch overlay, cloud integration, the SOC, and the operational technology edge.

catDistribution.metaDescription: The tracking console for the internet's most reliable logistics network: stray cats assigning themselves to humans. Enter your name; the System does the rest. Consent was never part of the protocol.
catDistribution.title: The Global Cat Distribution System
catDistribution.tagline: You do not choose the cat. The cat has already chosen.
catDistribution.intro: The Cat Distribution System is the internet's name for a well-documented phenomenon: you do not acquire a stray cat, a stray cat acquires you. This console tracks your assignment. Enter your name (city optional, the System knows anyway) and read the delivery manifest. Assignments are deterministic: the same name always receives the same cat. That is not a bug. That is destiny.
catDistribution.emptyHint: Enter a name. The System is patient. The System is always patient.
catDistribution.stampSub: Resistance is not filed under available options. Prepare a warm surface and lower your expectations of furniture.
catDistribution.creditNote: The Cat Distribution System is genuine internet folklore: the observation, popularized in the early 2020s, that stray cats appear precisely when and where they decide to. No cats were algorithmically generated; all cats are real and currently on their way.

importanceMeter.metaDescription: Measures how much of your attention a thing has actually earned. The arithmetic is real.
importanceMeter.title: Importance Meter
importanceMeter.tagline: Measures, to a defensible standard, the importance a topic has actually earned.
importanceMeter.intro: Enter the matter and its circumstances. Each factor is weighted, the weights are shown, and the subtotal is genuinely computed - it will move as you change things, sometimes dramatically. The subtotal is then multiplied by the bearing the matter has on the work you are accountable for. Results are reproducible.
importanceMeter.urgentLabel: URGENT appears in the subject line, in capitals
importanceMeter.ccLabel: People copied who did not need to be
importanceMeter.escalationLabel: How far it has been escalated
importanceMeter.raisedLabel: Raised in a meeting you were not invited to
importanceMeter.movedLabel: The deadline has already moved once
importanceMeter.coefficientNote: This coefficient is a constant. It is not affected by any input above, and it has never been observed to take another value.

remarks.trivial: Nothing here registers. Unusual, and slightly suspicious.
remarks.elevated: Elevated. Somebody has begun using capital letters.
remarks.considerable: Considerable. There is now a recurring meeting about it.
remarks.spectacular: Spectacular. This will be referred to for years as a lesson, by people who were not involved.

importanceMeter.methodBody: The weights above are arbitrary but consistent: identical inputs always produce an identical subtotal, which is the only property this needed. Nothing is rounded to reach the result and nothing is discarded. The subtotal is multiplied by the coefficient and the product is reported exactly. This tool computes rather than guesses, in keeping with the rest of the site. It happens to be computing something whose answer does not vary.
importanceMeter.gaugeAria: Result gauge. The needle rests at zero.
importanceMeter.overrideHint: The coefficient has resisted every attempt to change it through the interface. Whether it can be changed by other means is not documented.
importanceMeter.disclaimerBody: If English is not your first language: “zero fucks given” is a common informal expression meaning complete indifference — that something does not concern you in the slightest. It is vulgar, and it is used humorously far more often than aggressively, usually about bureaucracy, pointless urgency and work theatre rather than about people. The idea is not particular to English. Most European languages have their own idiom for the same shrug, built variously from food, animals, weather or anatomy, and several are a good deal more colourful than the English one. Register matters more than the words: it belongs in casual speech among people who know each other, and not in professional writing, a customer email or anything with your employer’s name on it.

vendor.title: Vendors
vendor.intro: Companies that make the product. Most of this timeline is here, because most of the industry's stories are about somebody building a thing and then discovering what it was for.

distributor.title: Distributors
distributor.intro: Two-tier distribution: they sell to resellers rather than to the organisations that use the equipment. An invisible layer to most engineers, and the one that decides which products are practical to buy in a given country.

reseller.title: Resellers and integrators
reseller.intro: The companies that actually install the thing. They carry other people's products, and their skill is in making a portfolio assembled for commercial reasons behave like a system.

services.title: Services and consulting
services.intro: Outsourcing, consulting, managed operations. They sell people and process rather than product, which is a harder thing to explain to a market and a harder thing to scale.

carrier.title: Carriers
carrier.intro: Operators that move somebody else's traffic. The physical substrate everything above them assumes, and the reason several entries here are really about rights of way and undersea cable.

datacentre.title: Data centres and interconnection
datacentre.intro: Colocation, hosting and the places networks meet. Property businesses with network effects, which is a stranger combination than it sounds.

training.title: Training and certification
training.intro: The companies and bodies that decide what competence looks like and who is allowed to claim it. On a site built by an instructor these are not a footnote.

standards.title: Standards, research and protocols
standards.intro: Not companies selling anything, or not only that: the laboratories, foundations and specifications the commercial entries are built on top of.

industryTags.milestonesLink: Before any of these companies: the milestones they were built on

milestones.title: Milestones: the ground the industry stands on
milestones.intro: The company timeline begins in the nineteenth century almost by accident. This page is the other history: the physics and engineering that had to exist first, from a stack of zinc and copper discs in 1800 to the first fibre laid across the Atlantic.
milestones.test: The test for inclusion here is narrow and deliberate. Not "important events in science", but: could a network engineer's working day be explained without it? Induction, amplification, Shannon's channel capacity, random access, packet switching. Things upstream of the job rather than beside it. Every entry says why it matters, not only what happened.
milestones.backToCompanies: The companies that were built on top of this

electricity.name: Electricity
electricity.blurb: Making it, moving it, and working out what it is. Five results between 1800 and 1887 that turn a curiosity into a field, ending with the demonstration of waves that had been predicted on paper twenty years earlier.

electronics.name: Electronics
electronics.blurb: Controlling it. The step from conducting a signal to acting on one: rectification, then amplification, then doing both in solid state, then doing it a million times on one piece of silicon.

digital.name: Digital
digital.blurb: Representing information as discrete symbols and reasoning about it rigorously. Three papers, two of them by the same person, that between them define what a computer is, what it cannot do, and how much can be sent down a noisy wire.

storage.name: Storage
storage.blurb: Keeping it. The arc from sequential to addressable to solid-state, each step changing not just capacity but what a system can reasonably assume about how long a read takes.

transfer.name: Transfer
transfer.blurb: Moving it. From the first separation of a message from its messenger to the fibre under the ocean, by way of the two design decisions - packets rather than circuits, and internetworking rather than one network - that produced everything since.
